# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-7 (Extended v82)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826. **Current narrative point (Autumn Year 2, approximately late 1825 or late 1826)**: Valjean and Cosette in sanctuary at Convent of Petit-Picpus. Earlier markers: 1815 (Bishop's 75th birthday, Valjean's theft and flight; Waterloo/Hougomont June 17-18); 1817 (young Parisians' Saint-Cloud excursion); 1818 spring (Montfermeil, Thénardier family, Fantine's arrival); 1819-1821 (Madeleine's mayoral tenure); **1823 January (Fantine's arrest; Javert's revelation; TRIAL SEQUENCE in Arras; Valjean's self-revelation; acquittal of Champmathieu; arrest issued; RETURN TO M. SUR M. before six a.m.; Fantine's death; Valjean arrested beside death-bed; VALJEAN ESCAPES same evening)**; December 1823 (Montfermeil rescue of Cosette, 1,500-franc payment to Thénardier); **December 26, 1823 (Valjean and Cosette returned to Paris via Barrier Monceaux)**; 1824 spring onward (decrepit building lodging; winter passed; spring advanced); **Summer Year 2**: Achieved sanctuary inside walled garden compound, le Petit-Picpus district. **1819-1825 (Six-year span during Prioress Mademoiselle de Blemeur's tenure)**. **1820 or 1821 (Madame de Genlis's brief residence attempt)**. **1824 (Nun of Sainte-Aure's death; only doll of her order remains)**. **1847 (Future reference: Mother Présentation became prioress)**.

## Primary Locations
M. sur M.; Montfermeil (between Livry and Chelles); **English harbor towns** (Dunstead, Yarlby, Kelford, Ravenmere, Staveford); Arras; Waterloo; Toulon; Paris districts including Mouffetard quarter (Rue Censier, Rue Copeau, Rue du Battoir-Saint-Victor, Rue du Puits l'Ermite, Rue de Pontoise; commissary office No. 14; Saint-Étienne-du-Mont church); **Gorbeau House** (Rue de la Cosette area, Mouffetard): Decrepit lodging, old woman portress, Javert's surveillance station. **Mouffetard escape**: Street lantern rope cut; Javert misled toward Cul-de-Sac Genrot. **LE PETIT-PICPUS DISTRICT**: Between Faubourg Saint-Antoine and la Râpée; market-gardens, timber-yards, unpaved roads; ancient street names (Droit-Mur formerly Rue des Églantiers; Aumarais formerly Maugout Lane). **Number 62 Rue Petit-Picpus (CONVENT CARRIAGE GATE)**: Ajar gate, courtyard, vine-hung walls, tall trees above wall. **Wall (approximately 18 feet)**: Extends from niche to house 49 Rue Polonceau; shorter fragment along Rue Droit-Mur. **CONVENT COMPLEX - THREE BUILDINGS**: (1) **Great Convent**: Inhabited by Bernardines-Benedictines nuns; gloomy building, heavily shuttered window with sheet zinc, ancient cistern pipes, linden-tree with ivy, grated windows, upper story scuttles resembling prison cells. (2) **Boarding-school**: Where scholars lodged. (3) **Little Convent**: Building with garden housing aged nuns of various orders destroyed in Revolution—relics from multiple communities (black, gray, white habits); established by government permission under Empire; government paid small pensions; reception cordial. **INTERIOR GARDEN (Great Convent)**: Vast oblong area; alley of large poplars; forest trees in corners; solitary gnarled tree, fruit-trees, vegetable beds, melon patch with glass frames, old well, stone benches, grass and green mould. **PARLOR (Great Convent)**: Theatre-box-like narrow space; monstrous lattice of iron bars (squares less than 1.5 inches diagonal) riveted by clenched-fist fastenings; behind lattice: barrier of black shutters reinforced with gingerbread-yellow wooden beams, always closed; behind shutters: nun's voice screened by iron grating and plate with thousand holes; slat opens revealing nun's mouth and chin only, covered with black veil, guimpe, shroud; window on world-side only; quadrangular hole one foot square with interlacing iron bars reinforced by sheet of tin with thousand microscopic holes; aperture like letter-box orifice; tape attached to bell-wire.

## Convent Communication System
**Bell-Telegraph Network**: Rule of silence withdrew speech from human creatures; speech bestowed on inanimate objects—church-bell and gardener's bell. Sonorous bell beside portress, audible throughout house, indicated by varied peals (acoustic telegraph) all material-life actions to be performed. Each person and thing had own peal: prioress one-and-one; sub-prioress one-and-two; six-five announced lessons (pupils said "go to six-five"); four-four was Madame de Genlis's signal (heard frequently, called "le diable a quatre"). **Nine strokes announced great event: opening of door of seclusion—frightful sheet of iron bristling with bolts, turned on hinges only in presence of archbishop**.

## Convent of the Bernardines of the Perpetual Adoration (Comprehensive Details)
**Order Lineage**: Bernardines-Benedictines of Martin Verga obedience; **1657 (Pope Alexander VII authorized by special brief Bernardines of Rue Petit-Picpus to practice Perpetual Adoration like Benedictine nuns of Holy Sacrament); two orders remained distinct**. Benedictine order founded 529 by Saint-Benoît; spawned nine orders including Cîteaux (1098), Carthusians, Cluny, Saint-Maur, Vallombrosa, Granmont, Célestins, Camaldules, Humiliés, Olivateurs, Silvestrins. **Note**: Not to be confused with Benedictine nuns of Cîteaux or Benedictines of Rue du Temple (different order with brown curtains, polished-wood-floor salon, white muslin windows, framed paintings, unveiled nun portrait, painted bouquets, Turk's head); mounted back to Abbé of Saint-Germain des Prés as ladies of Sacred Heart go back to Jesuits general and sisters of charity to Lazarists general. **Dress**: Black clothing with white guimpe mounting to chin; serge robe with large sleeves; large woollen veil; band descending over brow; novices wear all-white; professed nuns wear rosary at side. **Austerity**: Fast all year; abstain from meat; additional fasting in Lent; rise one to three a.m. for breviary and matins; sleep year-round on straw between serge sheets; never light fires; never bathe; scourge every Friday; strict silence except brief recreation; wear drugget chemises September 14 (Exaltation of Holy Cross) to Easter—originally year-round but modified due to summer fevers; resumed chemise causes three-to-four-day fever. **Vows**: Obedience, poverty, chastity, perseverance in seclusion. **Operational Rules**: Never see officiating priest (hidden behind nine-foot serge curtain); drop veils during sermons; speak low; walk with eyes down; only diocesan archbishop permitted entry; absolute passive submission to prioress (canonical subjection—at Christ's voice, at gesture, at first sign, immediately with cheerfulness, perseverance, blind obedience, like file in workman's hand); cannot read or write without express permission. **Reparation Practice**: Each nun in turn performs twelve-hour continuous reparation prayer (either 4 p.m. to 4 a.m. or 4 a.m. to 4 p.m.) on knees on stone before Holy Sacrament, hands clasped, rope around neck; when fatigue unbearable, prostrates flat against earth, arms outstretched as cross. **Possessions Rule**: Never say "my"; call everything "our"; if grow attached to petty object, must surrender it immediately. **Lodging**: Cells open; when meeting, one says "Blessed and adored be the most Holy Sacrament of the altar!" other responds "Forever!". **Hourly Bells**: At each hour three supplementary church bell strokes; all interrupt activity and say in unison formula praising Most Holy Sacrament. **Chanting**: Chant offices to solemn psalmody, pure Gregorian chant, full voice throughout; for office of dead adopt tone so low women's voices can barely descend—effect striking and tragic. **Burial Issue**: Vault beneath grand altar for community burials; Government forbids coffin burial in vault, so nuns leave convent when die. **Friday Observances**: High mass, vespers, all offices as on Sunday; observe little festivals; stations in chapel interminable. **Visitor Communication**: Prioress alone holds communication with strangers; permission to men always refused. **Men Allowed in Convent (Three Only)**: Archbishop, chaplain Abbé Banés (old and ugly; pupils could contemplate through choir grating), drawing-master M. Ansiaux/Anciot (described as frightful old hunchback). **Profession Ceremony**: Novice crowned with white roses, hair brushed and curled; prostrates self; great black veil thrown over her; office for dead sung; nuns separate into two files saying "Our sister is dead" and "Our sister is alive in Jesus Christ!". **Pupils**: Conform to all practices except austerities; some former pupils never break habit of saying "forever!" when door knocked; many wept seeking embrace permissions. **School Details (Écouen model)**: Distinctions made between virgins and florists in processions of Holy Sacrament; "dais" and "censors" held cords and carried incense; pupils sometimes picked forbidden fruit (green apples, spoiled apricots, inhabited pears) from garden alley with shabby fruit-trees, hiding them under pillows to eat in bed or in closets; young girls addressed daily question "Who is a virgin?". **Archbishop's Visit Observation**: During pastoral visit, pretty little rosy girl with beautiful golden hair entered class-room. **Mademoiselle Bouchard Incident**: Connected with Montmorency family; wagered she would request day's leave of absence (enormity in austere community); when Archbishop M. de Quélen passed pupils, she stepped out of ranks and asked; he smiled, granted three days; prioress could do nothing; caused horror of convent but joy of pupil. **School Mysticism**: Pupils taught prayer "Little white Paternoster, which God made" containing elaborate imagery of angels, Virgin Mary, apostles, virgins, shirts of God's birth, Saint Margaret's cross, encounters with Saint John, promise of paradise. **Choir Practice**: Mother Sainte-Mechtilde directs singing; selects seven pupils aged ten to sixteen of assorted voices and sizes, arranged by age from smallest to largest—creates visual effect of reed-pipe or living Pan-pipe of angels. **Pedagogical Practice**: Nuns severe only toward themselves; fire lighted only in school; food choice compared to convent; lavish thousand cares on scholars; when child approaches nun, nun never replies. **Restoration-Era Decline**: At beginning of Restoration, convent in decay—part of general death of religious orders after eighteenth century, disappearing; contemplation one of humanity's needs like prayer, but touched by Revolution will transform from hostile to social progress becoming favorable to it.

## Prioress and Vocal Mothers (1819-1825 Period)
**Mademoiselle de Blemeur (Mother Innocente)** (Prioress, 1819-1825): Age ~sixty; short, thick; "singing like a cracked pot"; excellent woman; only merry one in convent, adored for this; learned, erudite, wise, competent; proficient in history; crammed with Latin, Greek, Hebrew; more Benedictine monk than nun; descended from Marguerite de Blemeur, author of _Lives of the Saints of the Order of Saint-Benoît_; re-elected. **Vocal Mothers**: Mother Sainte-Honorine; Mother Sainte-Gertrude (treasurer); Mother-Saint-Ange (assistant mistress of novices); Mother Annonciation (sacristan); Mother Saint-Augustin (nurse; only malicious one); Mother Sainte-Mechtilde (Mademoiselle Gauvain; very young; beautiful voice; directs singing and choir); Mother des Anges (Mademoiselle Drouet; previously in Filles-Dieu and du Trésor convents); Mother Saint-Joseph (Mademoiselle de Cogolludo); Mother Sainte-Adélaide (Mademoiselle d'Auverney); Mother Miséricorde (Mademoiselle de Cifuentes; could not resist austerities); Mother Compassion (Mademoiselle de la Miltière; received at age sixty against rule; very wealthy); Mother Providence (Mademoiselle de Laudinière); Mother Présentation (Mademoiselle de Siguenza; future prioress 1847); Mother Sainte-Céligne (sister of sculptor Ceracchi; went mad); Mother Sainte-Chantal (Mademoiselle de Suzon; went mad).

## Resident Women in Little Convent
**Madame Albertine**: Woman not a nun, treated with great respect; ~thirty years old; dark complexion; tolerably pretty; possessed "arrangements of fortune necessary for a great marriage"; passed for dead in world; said to be mad; vague look in large black eyes; could she see—doubt about this; glided rather than walked; never spoke; uncertain whether she breathed; nostrils livid and pinched; possessed strange spectral grace; wherever she entered, people felt cold; touching her hand like touching snow. **Connection**: Once uttered "Ah! Auguste!" revealing knowledge of M. de Rohan (Vicar-general, awaiting episcopate); evident she belonged to very highest society, knew him familiarly, suggesting close relationship. **Other Resident Women**: Madame Beaufort d'Hautpoul, Marquise Dufresne, unnamed woman called Madame Vacarmini by pupils (formidable nose-blowing noise). **Centenarian from Abbey of Fontevrault**: Talked much of M. de Miromesnil (Keeper of Seals under Louis XVI) and Presidentess Duplat (intimate friend); pleasure and vanity to drag in these names on every pretext; told wonders of Abbey of Fontevrault like a city with streets in monastery; spoke with Picard accent amusing pupils; solemnly renewed vows yearly, at oath moment said to priest "Monseigneur Saint-François gave it to Monseigneur Saint-Julien, Monseigneur Saint-Julien gave it to Monseigneur Saint-Eusebius, Monseigneur Saint-Eusebius gave it to Monseigneur Saint-Procopius, etc., etc.; and thus I give it to you, father"—school-girls laughed under veils, charming little stifled laughs making vocal mothers frown; claimed in her youth Bernardine monks were every whit as good as mousquetaires—spoke eighteenth century through her; told of custom of four wines in Champagne and Bourgogne before Revolution: when great personage (marshal, prince, duke, peer) traversed town, city fathers presented four silver gondolas with four wine sorts inscribed monkey wine, lion wine, sheep wine, hog wine—expressing four stages descended by drunkard: intoxication (enlivens), irritation, dulling, brutalization. **Madame de Genlis** (attempted 1820-1821): Editing periodical _l'Intrépide_; requested residence; Duc d'Orléans recommended; vocal-mothers troubled (she had written romances); declared self first to detest them, had reached fierce devotion stage; with God's aid and Prince's help, entered; departed end of six or eight months, alleging no shade in garden; nuns delighted; very old but played harp well. **Madame de Genlis's Superstition**: Superstitious Latinist; pasted five lines Latin verse in red ink on yellow paper inside cupboard in cell where locked silverware and jewels; believed verses possessed property of frightening robbers; sixth-century Latin; raised question whether two thieves of Calvary named Dismas and Gestas or Dismas and Gesmas; orthography might have confounded Vicomte de Gestas's pretensions to descent from wicked thief; useful virtue of verses forms article of faith in order of Hospitallers. **Nun of Sainte-Aure**: Only survivor of her order; ancient convent of ladies of Sainte-Aure occupied this same house at beginning of eighteenth century before Benedictines of Martin Verga; too poor to wear magnificent habit (white robe with scarlet scapulary); piously put it on little manikin, exhibited with complacency, bequeathed to house at death; **1824: only one nun of order remained; currently: only doll remains**.

## Clerical Visitor: M. de Rohan
**Identity and Status**: Vicar-general of Archbishop of Paris, awaiting episcopate. **Habit**: Came tolerably often to celebrate offices in chapel of nuns of Petit-Picpus. **Appearance**: Had sweet and rather shrill voice; former mousquetaire; said to be very coquettish; handsome brown hair well dressed in roll around head; broad girdle of magnificent moire; black cassock of most elegant cut in world. **Effect on Pupils**: Held great place in imaginations of sixteen-year-old girls; could not see him because of serge curtain. **Connection**: Madame Albertine intimately familiar with him (called him "Auguste").

## Jean Valjean's Current Sanctuary Status
**ESCAPE FROM M. SUR M.** (January 1823 evening): Successfully fled jail after Javert's arrest beside Fantine's death-bed; climbed 18-foot wall using muscular force; placed Cosette on back; descended safely to interior garden via roof. **REFUGE DISCOVERY AND FAUCHELEVENT**: Encountered elderly crippled gardener Fauchelevent, admitted to convent approximately two years previously (1821) on Mayor Madeleine's recommendation after falling from cart. **PSYCHOLOGICAL STATE**: So long as Cosette near, needs nothing except her, fears nothing except her; experiencing continual tremor. **COSETTE**: Now sleeping in Fauchelevent's bed; rosy; completely dependent on Valjean. **CURRENT LOCATION** (Autumn Year 2): Still secured in convent sanctuary. **ALTERED APPEARANCE**: Sadness, uneasiness, anxiety, depression have altered his walk and impressed senility on bearing.

## Fauchelevent (Elderly Gardener—Established Ally)
**Identity**: Old crippled gardener; admitted to convent approximately two years previously on Valjean's (Mayor Madeleine's) recommendation after cart accident. **Character**: Grateful, talkative, excitable; calls Valjean "Father Madeleine"; speaks freely about work. **Current Occupation**: Spreading straw mats over melon beds in garden; wears bell and kneecap device. **Hospitality**: Provided Cosette safe bed; offered cheese, black bread, wine. **Status**: Valjean's only known ally and protector in Paris; sole person aware of Valjean and Cosette's presence.

## Javert's Pursuit and Strategic Hesitation
**REASSIGNMENT TO PARIS** (January 1823): When Valjean escaped M. sur M. jail, Javert summoned; attached to Paris police force. **NEWSPAPER REPORT** (December 1823): Newspaper announced Valjean's death; Javert read, remarked "That's a good entry," thought no more. **REACTIVATION**: Police report concerning child abduction in Montfermeil revived Javert's memory; suspected Valjean had sought daughter. **JAVERT'S SECRET INVESTIGATION**: Without telling anyone, took coach to Montfermeil; followed mysterious lodger to Gorbeau house; got old woman portress talking—she confirmed coat-lined-with-millions episode; hired room, listened at lodger's door; Valjean saw candle through key-hole, foiled spy by silence. **REASONS FOR SECRECY** (Three Motives): (1) Slightest indiscretion might alert Valjean; (2) Recapturing ex-convict reputed dead was magnificent success—feared being deprived; (3) Javert, being artist, had taste for unforeseen—hated well-heralded successes, preferred elaborating masterpieces in dark, unveiling suddenly. **PURSUIT ESCALATION**: Following day Valjean noticed five-franc piece falling; old woman suspected lodger intending to leave, warned Javert; at night Javert waited behind trees with two men. **ESCAPE FROM MOUFFETARD**: Valjean cut street lantern rope; Javert found disorder in lantern, led astray toward Cul-de-Sac Genrot. **JAVERT'S HESITATION AND PSYCHOLOGICAL TORMENT**: Followed Valjean from tree to tree, had not lost sight single instant; why had not arrested? Still in doubt. **STRATEGIC CALCULATION**: Considered abrupt demand for papers risky—if not Valjean, possibly chief of dangerous band; to arrest hastily would "kill the hen that laid golden eggs." Began the game—experienced ecstatic and infernal moment; allowed man to go ahead, knowing had him safe, gloating with voluptuousness of spider allowing fly to flutter, of cat letting mouse run; claws and talons possess monstrous sensuality. **MOMENT OF LOSS**: Even when saw Valjean escaped, Javert did not lose head; sure convict could not be far off, established sentinels, organized traps and ambuscades. **IMPEDIMENT TO ARREST**: Free press embarrassed police; arbitrary arrests denounced by newspapers; interference with individual liberty grave matter; police agents afraid of mistakes; mistake meant dismissal.

## English Harbor Towns Communities (Secondary Setting—Recurring Pattern)
**Named residents**: Matho Stenson, Ismira Stenson, Pelde Stenson, Harine Lindmere, Davus Stenworth, Havus Stenworth, Yera, Orrald the Younger, Orrald Stenson, Fewyn Stenworth, Volia Brackick, Nelan Brackick. **Towns/Locations**: Dunstead (fire at granary, set on purpose—revealed in letter Matho burned after reading), Yarlby (Matho and Ismira Stenson moved there, did not return; others followed within month), Kelford, Ravenmere, Staveford. **Observations and Activities**: Reading almanacs aloud with mispronounced saints (Matho); sorting letters by candlelight; discussing weather, harvest, lame horse, salt prices (Davus and Yera—"price of salt is scandal"); Harine and Orrald noted river up in spring; aching back complaints (Davus); baker's boy late, line at oven long; rain threatening since morning but holding off; bees humming in lavender; frost silvered hedges; wind from water with salt and tar smell; Pelde hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step; cart loaded with turnips creaked past well; children chased hoop down lane shrieking; smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields; Orrald bought ribbon at stall, regretted it; Harine argued with carter over sack of oats price; Pelde walked long way round to avoid muddy square; Pelde watched clouds, predicted rain wrongly; Harine mended torn sleeve by window, said little; Orrald talked for weeks of going to Gulhaven, yet in end stayed where he was; Pelde remarked river up again, Harine said always was in spring; gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps; light went early time of year. Volia and Nelan talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse. Somewhere dog barked at nothing and went quiet.
